cells.tense: You are here where the meaning is being passed along, pen in your own hand.
cells.act: gather the scattered thoughts into one line
cells.ask: Before your people next gather, pull your thinking about it down to a single line, however short. Carry that line through the whole occasion, and set it down first, before anything else you do there.
cells.core:
Gladness between people is real, and where a meaning is still being handed along, you can feel it move — you start to say what the whole thing means to you, and the warmth grows when it passes on. That place also hands you plenty to sort: what it's for, what it's become, who's holding it. The catch is the plenty. Your thinking about it scatters, some of it in your head and some of it outside.

Before you next walk in, gather the pieces into one sentence about what this is for you. Then hold that sentence under everything else you do there. The whole evening stays open; you get to stand in a single place while you carry it. That isn't a verdict on the evening. It's the one load you've chosen to put weight on.
cells.sheetLine: Warmth grows when it passes between people.

cells.tense: You will be bracing for the gathering that hasn't happened yet, writing it before it can.
cells.act: commit to the long build and do today's part
cells.ask: Choose one small part of how your people gather and do today's piece of it. Tomorrow, the next piece. Same part, no redesign.
cells.core:
You write the gathering before it can happen. Who'll come, who won't, what it'll mean, whether it lands. So the gladness you actually know — between people, real — gets kept in the future, where you can't stand in it. What this is for is you being there, not arranging there.

So choose one small part of how your people gather and do today's piece of it. Then tomorrow. Bring what actually happened with you to the next occasion, and keep your own account of why this belongs to you in the telling. Built this way, it gets handed on without your needing to rewrite it first. That doesn't take speed. It takes staying.

cells.tense: You stood at that door already, and you are still standing there.
cells.act: read the hardest page of it twice, slowly, before you stop
cells.ask: Take the part of your tradition that's hardest on you — the piece you don't get, or don't agree with — and sit with it twice through, slowly, before you stop. Nothing after.
cells.core:
A shared tradition keeps moving around you, and you've been holding back from it — half in, at the edge of a doorway that has your name on it. Gladness others make together reaches you, and you haven't been answering it. Nobody can hear that part for you.

Going all the way into the thing itself brings you close again; forcing yourself to join doesn't. Take the part of your tradition that's hardest on you — the piece you don't get, or don't agree with — and sit with it twice through, slowly, before you stop. Read it, and stop there. You're meeting the depth of the thing rather than the surface politeness of it, and depth doesn't ask you to belong first. What's yours returns through attention before it returns through the door.

cells.tense: Your pen is already moving here while you say you hold nothing.
cells.act: bring the two sides of your thinking into one plan
cells.ask: For a gathering you keep going to, name what you need from it and what it needs from you, and set both down as one short plan. Two lines is plenty.
cells.core:
A tradition keeps going, and you're in it. Recipes, dates, the words used, who gets asked. Ask and you'll say you were just showing up, keeping the usual thing going. But the usual thing keeps going because somebody keeps it, and by the look of it that somebody has been you.

So make one line you can hold. For a gathering you go to anyway, say what you need from it and what it needs from you, and set both down as one short plan — two lines is plenty. Do it so your own hand shows in it. The meaning those people celebrate carries your fingerprints too. Written that way, walking in feels different: you're not following a practice, you're keeping one.
